section_summary: This section concludes a Japan Institute publication on Japanese postal rules, includes a separate Institute promotional brochure, and contains State Department correspondence concerning translated scholarship and the suppression of Japanese magazines. Most of the section consists of a December 1943 FORTUNE reprint analyzing Japan’s wartime economic and strategic predicament and, in Karl Löwith’s companion essay, Japanese intellectual traditions, Zen Buddhism, Shinto, imperial loyalty, and attitudes toward death and sacrifice. The accompanying correspondence presents the articles as background for officials planning the war against Japan.

subfiles.title: Japan Institute answers on Japanese postal prohibitions and parcel-post rates (conclusion)
subfiles.doc_type: Informational bulletin article with institutional back matter
subfiles.about: The conclusion of an informational article explains Japanese restrictions on mailed matter and domestic parcel-post charges.
subfiles.summary: The article summarizes Japanese postal rules prohibiting subversive or immoral literature, dangerous materials, poisons, disease-bearing matter, currency sent outside declared-value post, and articles likely to harm postal workers or other mail. It notes that several prohibitions have regulated exceptions and supplies parcel-post rates for Japan proper and the colonies. The closing institutional page advertises the Japan Institute’s inquiry service, reference library, and free lending of films, slides, maps, records, and illustrated materials.

subfiles.title: Japan Institute: Clearing House for Information on Japan
subfiles.to: Educational institutions, organizations, researchers, and interested individuals
subfiles.about: A brochure describes the Japan Institute’s purpose, collections, sponsorship, and free information services.
subfiles.summary: The Institute presents itself as a clearinghouse intended to overcome the language barrier facing Americans seeking reliable information about Japan. Its holdings include Japanese- and English-language books, pamphlets, newspapers, periodicals, films, slides, and photographs. Sponsored by Tokyo’s Kokusai Bunka Shinkokai, it also maintains contacts with Japanese research institutes, libraries, and scholars and generally provides its services free of charge.

subfiles.title: Letter acknowledging translations from Nagao Ariga’s La Guerre Russo-Japonaise
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Hamilton thanks the correspondent for translated extracts from Nagao Ariga’s work and requests two additional copies.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges a May 21, 1942 letter enclosing translated extracts from Dr. Nagao Ariga’s La Guerre Russo-Japonaise. He expresses appreciation for the volume and asks for two more copies for interested officers of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting the discontinuation of three leading Japanese magazines
subfiles.about: Harriman relays a Red Star report that the Japanese publishers’ association had reduced six leading magazines to three.
subfiles.summary: The telegram cites a January 29 Red Star item based on a January 28 Tokyo dispatch. It reports that the Japanese publishers’ association discontinued Kaizō, Bungei Shunjū, and Nippon Hyōron while reducing the number of leading magazines from six to three. Harriman notes that the item did not appear in other newspapers.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding FORTUNE’s “Approaches to Tokyo” articles
subfiles.from: Albert T. Fisher II, FORTUNE Washington Office
subfiles.about: Fisher sends Hamilton FORTUNE articles examining Japan’s economy, war strategy, psychology, and possible approach to a negotiated settlement.
subfiles.summary: Fisher argues that the United States will eventually have to concentrate on an enemy whose actions and motivations remain poorly understood. He forwards FORTUNE’s December report, “Approaches to Tokyo,” because it studies the tactical, economic, and psychological problems involved in defeating Japan. He also offers additional copies for Hamilton’s associates.

subfiles.title: FORTUNE reprint: “The Japanese Predicament” and “The Japanese Mind”
subfiles.doc_type: Magazine reprint with contents and editorial statement
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and other readers
subfiles.about: The reprint analyzes Japan’s wartime economic and strategic vulnerabilities and presents Karl Löwith’s interpretation of Japanese mentality, culture, religion, and imperial loyalty.
subfiles.summary: “The Japanese Predicament” argues that Japan possesses a large empire and abundant resources but lacks the ships, industrial capacity, skilled labor, and organization needed to exploit and defend them. It predicts a retreat toward an inner fortress comprising Japan, Korea, Manchuria, North China, and Formosa, while warning that Japan might seek a negotiated settlement preserving indirect control over parts of its empire. In “The Japanese Mind,” Karl Löwith describes the uneasy coexistence of imported Western modernity with Japanese traditions derived from China, Buddhism, Zen, Shinto, ancestor worship, and imperial loyalty. The concluding pages reproduce FORTUNE’s December 1943 contents and an editorial memorandum by Ralph D. Paine Jr. defining the magazine’s wartime mission of informing American leaders about winning the war and planning the peace.
